Random Forest Kernel - Tutorial (RLT)

Ruoqing Zhu

Last Updated: October 26, 2026

Source: vignettes/articles/feature-kernel.Rmd
feature-kernel.Rmd

Overview

The random forest kernel describes which observations a fitted forest groups together. In the ordinary mode of forest.kernel(), each matrix entry counts the trees in which the corresponding pair shares a terminal node. These raw counts are not normalized observation weights for a forest prediction.

With both X1 and X2, the result has one row per observation in X1 and one column per observation in X2. Omitting X2 gives a self-kernel for X1.

Example 1 - Axis-aligned

We fit a regression forest with single-variable splits and compute leaf-sharing counts between a target point and the training observations. Setting nsplit = 0 searches all available cutpoints.

This example also uses vs.train = TRUE. That mode weights each tree’s leaf-sharing indicator by the reference observation’s in-bag multiplicity in that tree. It requires resample.track = TRUE when fitting and the original training data, in their original row order, as X2.

# ---- Generate a small dataset (about 100 obs) ----
set.seed(1)
n <- 120; p <- 5
X <- matrix(runif(n * p), n, p)
y <- X[, 1] + X[, 2] + rnorm(n)

# Train the forest with axis-aligned splits
library(RLT)
fit_rect <- RLT(
  X, y, model = "regression",
  ntrees = 300, mtry = p, nmin = 5,
  nsplit = 0,
  resample.prob = 0.8, resample.replace = TRUE,
  param.control = list("resample.track" = TRUE),
  ncores = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)

# Choose a target point
newX <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), 1, p)

# Leaf-sharing tree counts between newX and all X
KW_rect <- forest.kernel(fit_rect, X1 = newX, X2 = X)$Kernel

# Rescale counts only to set circle sizes in the plots
size_scale <- 10 * sqrt(KW_rect / sqrt(sum(KW_rect^2)))
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))

# X1 vs X2 (both are signal features)
plot(X[, 1], X[, 2], col = "deepskyblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Axis-aligned kernel - X1 vs X2")
points(X[, 1], X[, 2], col = "darkorange", cex = size_scale, lwd = 2)
points(newX[1], newX[2], col = "black", pch = 4, cex = 4, lwd = 5)
legend("bottomright", "Target Point", pch = 4, col = "black", lwd = 5, lty = NA, cex = 1.2)

# X1 vs X3 (X3 is noise)
plot(X[, 1], X[, 3], col = "deepskyblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Axis-aligned kernel - X1 vs X3")
points(X[, 1], X[, 3], col = "darkorange", cex = size_scale, lwd = 2)
points(newX[1], newX[3], col = "black", pch = 4, cex = 4, lwd = 5)

# Weight leaf sharing by each training observation's in-bag multiplicity
KW_rect_train <- forest.kernel(fit_rect, X1 = newX, X2 = X, vs.train = TRUE)$Kernel
size_scale_train <- 10 * sqrt(KW_rect_train / sqrt(sum(KW_rect_train^2)))
plot(X[, 1], X[, 2], col = "deepskyblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Axis-aligned kernel (vs.train=TRUE) - X1 vs X2")
points(X[, 1], X[, 2], col = "darkorange", cex = size_scale_train, lwd = 2)
points(newX[1], newX[2], col = "black", pch = 4, cex = 4, lwd = 5)

# Another projection
plot(X[, 2], X[, 3], col = "deepskyblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Axis-aligned kernel - X2 vs X3")
points(X[, 2], X[, 3], col = "darkorange", cex = size_scale, lwd = 2)
points(newX[2], newX[3], col = "black", pch = 4, cex = 4, lwd = 5)


par(op)

The panels show leaf sharing with the target at (X1, X2, X3) = (0.5, 0.3, 0.5). Orange circle size increases with the count. Compare the two X1/X2 panels to see the effect of in-bag multiplicity; the projections containing the noise variable X3 spread the highlighted observations along a direction that does not contribute to the simulated response. These are projections of a five-dimensional kernel, so distance to the cross in one panel does not fully determine leaf sharing.

The size_scale calculations rescale each kernel vector for plotting. They do not change the returned counts or produce prediction weights. Because each vector is rescaled separately, circle sizes across panels should be read relative to the other circles in the same panel.

Example 2 - Linear-combination

We next use sliced inverse regression (SIR) to estimate predictor directions for linear-combination splits. Setting linear.comb = 2 permits up to two variables in a direction, and nsplit = 3 compares three random candidate cutpoints along it.

This is a separate simulation with a different response, noise level, and resampling scheme. The two examples illustrate kernel structure, rather than provide a controlled comparison of split methods.

set.seed(1)
n <- 120; p <- 5
X <- matrix(runif(n * p), n, p)
y <- X[, 1] + X[, 3] + 0.3 * rnorm(n)

fit_lc <- RLT(
  X, y, model = "regression",
  ntrees = 300, mtry = p, nmin = 5,
  nsplit = 3,
  resample.prob = 0.9, resample.replace = FALSE,
  linear.comb = 2, linear.comb.method = "sir",
  ncores = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)

newX <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), 1, p)
KW_lc <- forest.kernel(fit_lc, X1 = newX, X2 = X)$Kernel
size_scale_lc <- 10 * sqrt(KW_lc / sqrt(sum(KW_lc^2)))
par(mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))
plot(X[, 1], X[, 3], col = "deepskyblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Linear-combination kernel - X1 vs X3")
points(X[, 1], X[, 3], col = "darkorange", cex = size_scale_lc, lwd = 2)
points(newX[1], newX[3], col = "black", pch = 4, cex = 4, lwd = 5)
legend("topright", "Target Point", pch = 4, col = "black", lwd = 5, lty = NA, cex = 1.2)

Here the response depends on the sum of X1 and X3. The plot shows which observations share terminal nodes with the target across the forest. Linear-combination splits can group observations along an oblique direction, so a large leaf-sharing count does not require each coordinate to be close to the target separately.

OOB Self-kernel

The separate oob = TRUE mode uses only trees in which both observations are out of bag. It requires retained resampling records and the original training data as X1, with X2 omitted. Unlike the ordinary counts shown above, its Kernel is normalized by the number of trees where both observations are OOB. The returned C and N matrices contain the leaf-sharing and joint-OOB counts; see forest.kernel().
